title: Song of the Volga Boatmen: Chaliapin, 1922 and 1927
work: Song of the Volga Boatmen, arranged by Chaliapin and Keneman
question: How does Chaliapin vary the boatmen’s repeated call across the song?
intro: Men hauling barges along the Volga sang to coordinate each heave. Chaliapin and Fyodor Keneman arranged their work song as a piece for bass and orchestra. Chaliapin returns again and again to the same short call, building it to a shout and then letting it die away.

recordings.label: Fyodor Chaliapin, George W. Byng
recordings.note: Chaliapin’s first recording of the arrangement he helped create, made through an acoustic horn with Byng conducting.

recordings.label: Fyodor Chaliapin, Albert Coates
recordings.note: The electrical remake, conducted by Coates, was made five years after Chaliapin’s first version.

passages.label: Crescendo on the repeated call
passages.note: The bass gives the repeated call more force, and the short phrases build into one long swell.

passages.label: Quieter phrases after the climax
passages.note: Chaliapin reaches the top of the crescendo, then sings the next phrases more quietly while the orchestra continues beneath him.

passages.label: Second crescendo
passages.note: The repeated call grows louder again. The bass holds the rise across successive phrases.

passages.label: Diminuendo to the close
passages.note: The voice grows quieter, and the last calls die away into the orchestral accompaniment.
